title: About Me
text:
I’m currently pursuing a Master of Applied Economics and Data Science at the University of Pennsylvania. I have 4+ years of experience working in economic consulting supporting complex commercial litigation and international arbitration across Latin America and the U.S., with a focus on valuation, damages quantification, and IP/antitrust disputes.
My experience includes applying economic modeling, econometrics, event study analysis and financial analysis to matters involving claims from USD 2M to over USD 100M. I also have experience working across the full litigation lifecycle, including discovery, expert report preparation, deposition, and trial support.
Technical skills: Python, R, Stata, Excel.

title: Understanding the Welfare Cost of Business Cycles
text:
Recessions feel painful. People lose jobs, incomes shrink, families cut back on spending. So it seems that eliminating business cycles altogether would make society much better off. In 1987, economist Robert Lucas asked, if we could eliminate all the ups and downs in the economy (keeping only the long-run growth trend) how much would people be willing to pay for that?
The answer was surprising: almost nothing. According to Lucas’ calculations, the average American would trade less than half a percent of their consumption to eliminate every recession and boom forever. This is the welfare cost of business cycles, and its surprisingly small size became a famous results in macroeconomics.
The key insight is a distinction between the level of consumption and its variability. Business cycles don’t (in Lucas’s framework) change how much people consume on average. Instead they just make consumption bounce up and down around a stable trend. A recession is followed, on average, by a recovery.
People dislike risk, but they dislike it because of diminishing marginal utility. Losing \(1,000\) hurts more than gaining \(1,000\) helps. So variability around a fixed average is costly, but only mildly costly, because the swings that make up actual business cycles are small relative to how much income grows decade after decade. Compare a typical recession which might reduce consumption by 2–3% for a year or two with long-term economic growth that raises consumption by a considerably larger magnitude.
Economists measure how much a household would pay to avoid risk using utility functions like:
\[u(c)=\frac{c^{1-\sigma}-1}{1-\sigma}\] where \(\sigma\) measures the risk aversion (the higher \(\sigma\), the higher the aversion to risk).
If consumption fluctuates with variance \(\sigma^2_c\) around a mean of \(1\), a standard approximation shows that the cost of business cycles, which is denoted as \(g\) and can be thought of as the fraction of consumption a household would sacrifice to make consumption perfectly stable, is approximately:
\[g\approx \frac{1}{2}\sigma \sigma^2_c\] This formula carries the whole intuition. The cost scales with the variance of consumption, multiplied by how risk-averse people are. Since actual measured consumption volatility is small (\(\sigma^2_c\) is on the order of a few tenths of a percent), even with fairly high risk aversion, \(g\) comes out small (only a fraction of one percent).
Lucas’s 1987 calculation landed at a pivotal moment. Since Keynes, much of macroeconomics had been built around the premise that smoothing business cycles through fiscal and monetary policy was the central task of the discipline. Lucas’s result flipped the priority, because if fluctuations barely matter for welfare, then the big prize is economic growth, not stabilization.
The result may not appear intuitive at first. Recessions feel devastating, especially to people who lose jobs or homes. Lucas’s calculation, however, uses aggregate, average consumption, which is remarkably smooth even during recessions (most people keep their jobs and incomes even in bad years). But the pain of a recession is concentrated: unemployment, foreclosure, and bankruptcy hit a minority of households very hard, while the majority barely notice. Averaging across everyone hides this uneven distribution.
Given these considerations, there have been decades of follow-up research. This research suggests that incorporating uninsurable individual-level risk, unemployment spells, effects of recessions on long-run growth, and the asymmetric nature of downturns all push the estimated welfare cost higher.
As a result of these new observations, a more recent consensus on Lucas’s calculation is that, though not wrong, it could be narrow. Incorporating the idea that real business cycles are not necessarily smooth, symmetric, or evenly felt to Lucas’ estimation might shed new insights as to how households deal with economic downturns in a more precise way.

title: Are bigger cities more expensive?
text:
Source: Von Deensel - Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires, CC BY 2.0


Big cities are assumed to cost more to live in. Tokyo, Shanghai and Delhi, surely all that scale drives prices up? I decided to test that assumption directly, and the answer turned out to be more interesting than a simple yes or no.
To do this, I pulled population data for the world’s largest cities from Wikipedia, then matched each one against Numbeo’s crowdsourced cost-of-living rankings. Numbeo’s database scores cities on prices for groceries, rent, restaurants, and more, all benchmarked against New York City (set at 100). Not every huge city has enough Numbeo data to be scored, so I widened my search until I found 100 large cities with reliable data, reaching as far as the 174th-largest city in the world to fill that quota, out of 479 cities Numbeo tracks overall. Considering this, it is important to note that my sample skews toward cities that are well-documented online, which tends to mean wealthier and more internationally connected cities. A lot of very large but less-tracked cities (particularly across parts of Africa and South Asia) simply didn’t have enough data for me to include.
For each city, I calculated a “value score” or local purchasing power divided by cost of living. This can be thought of as how far does a typical local salary actually stretch against local prices. A score above 1 means wages outpace costs and below 1 means the opposite.
Population size told me almost nothing about cost of living
When I ran the numbers, I found essentially no relationship between how big a city is and how expensive it is (see Figure 1). This correlation came out to -0.09, which is about as close to “no pattern” as real-world data gets. Some of the cheapest cities I measured (several mid-sized Indian cities) sit right alongside some of the world’s largest metros in population, while a few smaller cities on my list were nearly as pricey as New York. The old assumption that scale drives up cost simply doesn’t hold once I looked past a handful of famous outliers like Tokyo or Shanghai.






Figure 1



India’s mid-size tech hubs offer exceptional value
The top of my best-value list was dominated by Indian cities: Hyderabad topped the list with a value score of 7.1, followed by Pune, Chennai, and Bangalore all above 5 (see Figure 2). That means a typical local salary in Hyderabad buys roughly seven times more relative to living costs than the same ratio in a low-value city like Addis Ababa. Two Chinese cities, Chongqing and Chengdu, are also in my top 10. The takeaway here is that, for remote workers with location flexibility, employers setting cost-of-living-adjusted salaries, or companies scouting new office locations, these cities represent a genuinely underrated combination of large talent pools and strong purchasing power. This does not mean that they are just “cheap,” but cheap relative to what people there actually earn.






Figure 2



“Worst value” hid two very different stories
My bottom 10 split into two distinct groups, and the difference matters a lot in practice. Mexico City, Tehran, Cairo, Buenos Aires, and New York City itself all scored close to 1.0, meaning costs and local purchasing power are roughly balanced there (see Figure 3). That’s not necessarily bad, it is just average.
The real outliers I found were Abidjan and Addis Ababa, scoring 0.28 and 0.27, considerably lower than everywhere else on the list. Here’s the nuance I want to highlight: these cities aren’t expensive by sticker price (their cost-of-living index is actually moderate). What drags their score down is very low local purchasing power. Wages are simply too low relative to even modest costs. This is a distinct problem from high prices, and it might call for a different response. Anyone setting compensation for expat staff, aid workers, or business travelers in these cities should recognize that “moderate local prices” doesn’t mean affordability for the people who actually live there because local salaries aren’t providing the cushion that similar price levels would provide elsewhere.






Figure 3



The bigger picture
This analysis seems to suggest that it may be inaccurate to treat “big city” and “expensive city” as synonyms. They’re not the same axis at all. I’d argue that a better way to evaluate where money goes further (whether that is the result of relocation, international hiring, or just curiosity) is to look at purchasing power relative to cost, not cost in isolation. By that measure, some of the most attractive cities I found for stretching a dollar rarely make anyone’s “expensive city” headlines.
Full code, data, and README are available on GitHub: cost-of-living-scraper

title: Is AI replacing humans?
text:
Source: https://www.famouscampaigns.com/2025/06/make-ai-worried-youre-going-to-take-its-job-the-economist/


Worrying about AI replacing humans in the labor market may be one of the most common concerns among workers since the launch of ChatGPT in late November 2022. I wanted to see if there is any sign that generative AI has actually affected the labor market. Using IPUMS CPS data from 2019 to 2025 (three years prior and three years after the launch of ChatGPT), I focused my analysis on comparing employment outcomes for “computer occupations” (software developers, programmers, systems analysts, and similar roles) with overall employment outcomes (all occupations), using four visuals built from weighted CPS estimates.
The first insight is that among workers aged 22–29, tech unemployment sat low and stable through 2021, around 1.4–1.6%. Then, starting in 2022, it began climbing every single year, reaching roughly 4% by 2025 (see Figure 1).






Figure 1



That alone wouldn’t mean much, except that overall unemployment rate was moving in the opposite direction over the same period, spiking during the pandemic recovery, then falling steadily as the broader job market improved. The two lines essentially swap places right around 2022. I found the same crossover among workers 30 and older: tech unemployment bottoms out in 2022, then rises every year after, while overall unemployment stays flat (see Figure 2). This is a first indication that tells us that some specific factor is pulling on the tech occupations, a factor that is not necessarily having any incidence in the overall unemployment rate.






Figure 2



But the explanation does not seem to be that AI is making some jobs disappear. If AI were simply replacing tech workers, I’d expect to see computer occupations shrinking as a share of total employment. They aren’t (see Figure 3). Tech’s share of the workforce has held steady hovering between 3.5% and 4.2% the entire period, with only a slight dip in 2025. So whatever is happening, it isn’t tech jobs disappearing outright. It looks more like people already working in tech are having a harder time staying employed, or a harder time landing back on their feet once they lose a job.






Figure 3



At this point it seems important ruling out the obvious alternative explanation. For this, I checked whether young people are just giving up on work in general. If overall youth labor force participation were falling, the tech-unemployment rise might just be one symptom of a broader retreat of young people from the job market, which would indicate that there is no specific factor affecting tech jobs at all. However, according to the data, participation among 22–29 year-olds actually rose to a peak in 2023 and has held steady since (see Figure 4). Young workers are still out there, still looking for jobs. They’re just not landing tech jobs as easily as they used to.






Figure 4



So does this mean AI is the cause of the decline in employment in tech jobs? The timing lines up suggestively: the tech unemployment climb starts right as generative AI tools were taking off, but 2022 and 2023 were also messy years for entirely different reasons. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates aggressively starting in 2022 to fight inflation. Venture funding tightened, and a lot of tech firms pulled back hiring or cut staff as a result. On top of that, major tech companies including Meta, Amazon and Google that had overhired during the pandemic, ran large layoffs in 2022 and 2023. This situation was not particularly related to AI but rather was an effect of pandemic-era over-expansion.
Both of the previously described forces would produce a very similar pattern to the one I’m seeing from the data: rising tech unemployment, stable tech employment share. In order to untangle the different factors at play here would need more granular data, for example, task-level measures of how exposed specific jobs are to AI tools, for instance, rather than a broad occupation category.
The takeaway
The pattern of increased unemployment in tech jobs is consistent with generative AI’s market launch, but it’s important to highlight that this is a correlation with AI’s arrival, not proof of it. Rate hikes and layoff corrections are at least as plausible an explanation. The most likely explanation is that all three forces are tangled together. Separating them will require a more in-depth analysis.
Full code, data, and README are available on GitHub: AI and Jobs

text:
Source: Von Deensel - Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires, CC BY 2.0

title: Is Europe safer than the U.S.?
text:
Source: Scott G Winterton, Deseret News


Recent debates have brought to light the question of whether Europe is becoming less safe and whether the U.S. is actually safer in comparison. I set out to look for the data to try to have a better grasp of this debate. The first thing that I should note is that comparing crime across countries can be challenging because police record offenses differently. So I used the measure that travels best: homicide, counted from death certificates. The data I used covers the U.S. and 28 European countries (the European Union or EU plus the UK), averaged over 2018-2022. Country data comes from the World Health Organization (WHO) and state data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The headline is hard to miss. The U.S. homicide rate is about 6.8 homicides per 100,000 people a year. The population-weighted European average is 0.63, so the U.S. rate is roughly eleven times higher. Even Latvia, Europe’s highest at 3.4, is about half the U.S. figure. Lithuania and Estonia sit at 2.2, while Ireland (0.2), Germany, and the UK (both 0.4) are at the bottom (see Figure 1).






Figure 1



The gap between Europe and the U.S. didn’t open recently. In 2000, the U.S. rate was about four times Europe’s. By 2019 it was about nine times. Europe’s rate fell by more than half, from about 1.45 to 0.61, while the U.S. stayed between roughly 5 and 7 and then jumped to almost 8 in 2021 (see Figure 2). It is worth noting that I stop the European line at 2020 on purpose. After that year, WHO data is missing for large countries such as Germany. The weighted average would then move because of who is reporting, not because anything changed.






Figure 2



At first, you could think that the U.S. national number hides a few extremely violent states pulling up an otherwise more European-looking country. However, the data seem to suggest a different story (see Figure 3). The median U.S. state has a rate of about 6.2, roughly eight times Europe’s median country (0.75). All 51 jurisdictions (50 states plus D.C.) are above that European median, and 39 of them are above every European country. The spread is still huge. Mississippi (17.7) and Louisiana (around 17) are in a league of their own, and D.C. tops 25. At the other end, New Hampshire and Maine, at about 1.7, would still rank behind only the three Baltic states if they were European countries. This indicates that the national figure from the U.S. is not the consequence of a few outlier states with high homicide rates. Overall, the picture seems to suggest that the high homicide incidence in the U.S. is not a state-specific circumstance but rather a nationwide trend.






Figure 3



After seeing this trend, I wanted to understand why this could be happening and what other factors could be explaining this phenomenon. Of course, there are several plausible explanations for this. For the sake of brevity, I explore two usual suspects: wealth and inequality (see Figure 4). Within Europe, the relationships are weak. Richer countries have slightly lower homicide rates, and more unequal ones slightly higher rates. The U.S. is far above both. If I extend the European lines to the U.S. level of income and inequality, they predict rates of about 0.8 and 1.5. The actual figure is 6.85.
The inequality panel is interesting. With the U.S. in the top right corner, it looks like a strong upward relationship, and across all 29 countries the correlation is about 0.5. But one point is doing nearly all the work. Remove it, and the correlation among the 28 European countries is about 0.3. In this case, the single extreme observation of the U.S. can manufacture a trend. Based on this data, it seems that neither wealth nor inequality alone explains the U.S. gap.






Figure 4



It is important to remind ourselves here what that this is a descriptive rather than a causal analysis, therefore I was able show where and how large the gap is, but not why. Also, it is worth noting again that I measured just one variable associated with crime: homicide. There are additional variables associated with non-lethal violence that might be considered to have a more accurate picture of whether overall crime is in fact higher in the U.S. than in Europe.
The takeaway
In terms of homicide, the analysis seems to suggest that the U.S. isn’t Europe with a few bad states. Its typical state looks very different from Europe’s typical country, and the gap has widened over two decades. The obvious economic explanations, wealth and inequality, seem to leave most of the gap unexplained. This raises interesting questions about the causes of this large gap. An analysis that explores this will require a more in-depth exploration of additional factors.
Full code, data, and README are available on GitHub: Crime Comparison

title: Mapping crime in Philadelphia
text:
Source: Elevated Angles


I wanted to see in which parts of Philadelphia crime was worse to identify the most potentially dangerous parts of the city. So I mapped the data and tried to understand whether the pattern follows how much money households earn. To do this, I used Philadelphia Police Department incident reports from 2020 to 2024, covering every offense type, about 730,000 incidents in all. I averaged them to a typical year, then divided by each census tract’s population to get incidents per 1,000 residents. Census tracts are neighborhood-sized areas of a few thousand people, and using a rate keeps big and small areas comparable. For income, I used the Census Bureau’s median household income estimates for the same five years. I left out tracts with fewer than 500 residents, which left 387 tracts. Thirteen of those had no reliable income estimate.
On the crime map (see Figure 1), the darkest tracts (highest rates) cluster in a broad band through the middle of the city, including much of North Philadelphia, with more dark patches in West and Southwest Philadelphia. The lowest rates are mostly in the far Northeast and Northwest. Now look at the income map (see Figure 2), where darker also means higher. The lightest tracts (the lowest incomes) sit in that same central band.






Figure 1



The highest incomes show up in the Northwest and Northeast, the areas that look calmest on the crime map. Overall both maps paint a suggestive picture: areas in Philadelphia with higher crime rates are associated with lower median household income.






Figure 2



Now, as an initial approximation to understanding the information from the previous two maps, I plotted the relationship between income and crime (see Figure 3). On this plot, each dot is a tract. Moving right means higher income, and moving up means more crime per resident. The red line shows the typical trend. The plot shows that, at the low end, tracts with incomes around $20,000 average about 170 incidents per 1,000 residents a year. By roughly $70,000, that falls to about 60, a drop of around two-thirds. Past $70,000, the line goes flat. A tract at $150,000 looks about the same as one at $80,000.
This suggests that there isn’t a relationship that can be simplified to “more money, always less crime.” This rather looks more like a threshold: crime is much higher in the lowest-income neighborhoods, and income above the middle range doesn’t go with much further decline. The dots are also widely scattered. Among tracts near $40,000, rates run from under 50 to more than 500. Income explains part of the story, but not all of it.






Figure 3



It is worth noting the four blue dots floating above the pack. These are Center City tracts, with rates of roughly 300 to 700 average annual incidents, despite middle-to-high incomes. The likely explanation for these outlier dots lies in the math. Rates divide by residents, but Center City’s incidents involve commuters, shoppers, tourists and nightlife crowds. Few people live there and many pass through, so the rate looks inflated. That is a result of how I measured the variable, not evidence that wealthy residents there face more crime. These tracts may also tug the red line upward at higher incomes, so the flat stretch could be slightly exaggerated.
Though the previous figures point to a correlation between income and crime, it is important to remember that this relationship is just that: correlation, not causation. In this analysis, income likely stands in for other things like housing conditions, job access and public investment. Neighborhood averages say nothing about any individual household.
The takeaway
Reported crime in Philadelphia is concentrated in lower-income parts of the city, and the drop-off is steepest at the bottom of the income scale. But it is important to remember that income is only part of the picture, and that busy commercial districts break the pattern. A more in-depth analysis could also look at the relationship between income and violent crime and compare it with overall crime to determine if the type of crime changes the results of this analysis. Including additional variables (like unemployment rates and public investment by tract) may provide additional insights to the pattern presented here.
Full code, data, and README are available on GitHub: Crime in Philadelphia

title: Do Rich Parents Have Rich Kids? An SQL Tutorial to Match Parents and Children in Data
text:
Source: Markus Winkler


Since 1968, the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) has followed the same families, and then their children’s families. That makes it perfect for asking how much a parent’s income shapes a child’s. The catch, however, is that nothing in the data says “this is Ana’s mother.” You have to find the parents yourself, and SQL inside Python can be a useful tool for this type of analysis. What follows is a brief tutorial of how to do this.
Step 1: Give everyone a name tag
Every person is identified by two numbers: their family’s 1968 interview number (id68) and a person number (pn). Family IDs change every wave, so these 1968 numbers are the only stable labels. Combine them into one name tag: id681000+pn. A separate Parent Identification file lists each person’s birth mother and father with the same two numbers, 0 meaning “none.” Load both into SQLite:
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
ind.to_sql("individuals", con, index=False)
pid.to_sql("parent_ids", con, index=False)
Step 2: Find each child’s parents
NULLIF turns the 0s into NULLs, so nobody matches a parent who doesn’t exist:
CREATE TABLE parent_keys AS
SELECT id68*1000+pn AS person_id,
       NULLIF(mother_id68,0)*1000+NULLIF(mother_pn,0) AS mother_id,
       NULLIF(father_id68,0)*1000+NULLIF(father_pn,0) AS father_id
FROM parent_ids;
Now the clever part, a self-join. Picture persons (built the same way from individuals) as a phone book. For each child we look up the mother’s entry and the father’s entry in the same book, using two aliases, m and f:
CREATE TABLE child_parent AS
SELECT pk.person_id AS child_id, pk.mother_id, pk.father_id
FROM parent_keys pk
LEFT JOIN persons m ON pk.mother_id = m.person_id
LEFT JOIN persons f ON pk.father_id = f.person_id;
LEFT JOIN means “keep the child even if the parent isn’t in the book”. An INNER JOIN would quietly erase them and bias the sample. Then check with GROUP BY and HAVING that no child appears twice:
SELECT child_id, COUNT(*) FROM child_parent GROUP BY child_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
Zero rows means a clean match. Aggregation grades it too: SUM(mother_id IS NOT NULL) counts children with a known mother.
Step 3: Turn families into income
Income lives in yearly family files, and a family’s number changes every wave. So we reshape the wide individual file into one row per person per wave (UNION ALL), then JOIN on wave and family number to give each person-year their family’s income. Each income variable describes the previous calendar year, and we convert everything to 2016 dollars.
Parents are measured when the child was 15–19, and children at 30–40. One year, or many? For each person we rank observed years by closeness to a central age (17 for parents, 35 for children). Rank 1 is the snapshot. The average is the movie:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY child_id ORDER BY ABS(age - 35), age) AS rk
...
AVG(CASE WHEN rk = 1 THEN income END) AS single,  -- snapshot
AVG(income)                           AS multi    -- movie
GROUP BY child collapses the years into one row per child. We keep children with at least two parental years and three of their own, and drop incomes under $1,000 so logs work.
Step 4: How sticky is income?
Regress log child income on log parent income. The slope is the intergenerational elasticity (IGE): 0.46 means children of parents earning 10% more earn about 4.6% more.
fit = sm.OLS(np.log(d[y]), sm.add_constant(np.log(d[x]))).fit()

Swap a one-year parental snapshot for the movie and the estimate jumps by about 0.08. Averaging child income barely matters.
Step 5: When you take the photo matters
Now use child income at a single age (parents: multi-year; see table below):

At 25–30 the estimate is about 0.42; by 35 and 45 it reaches 0.51 and 0.55. That is life-cycle bias: young adults are still starting out, so their income says less about where they will end up. The pattern isn’t smooth (age 40 dips) and each age mixes different cohorts, so treat it as a hint.
Step 6: Why the movie beats the snapshot
Imagine photographing a family in the year Dad got a bonus, or Mom was laid off. That photo is long-run status plus luck. Luck in the variable you regress on dilutes the relationship and pulls the slope toward zero, so single-year parental income understates the IGE. Averaging years washes out much of the luck and leaves something closer to a family’s standard of living.

Is there a way to predict whether the economy is heading for a recession? Every few years, newspaper headlines ask this same question, usually based on the observed behavior of bond yields. I wanted to understand what, if anything, can bond yields signal about future recessions, and whether this signal is flashing now.
The first relevant finding is that it’s not about how high yields are. It’s about the shape of the curve. Bond yields change with the length of the loan. Normally, lending to the government for 10 years pays more than lending for 3 months, because you’re tying your money up for longer. That gap, the spread, is usually positive. Sometimes it flips. Short-term yields rise above long-term ones, and the curve is “inverted.” Investors are saying they expect rates to fall later, usually because the economy is weakening. That’s the recession signal.
To understand what history says about this, I pulled U.S. Treasuries spread data since 1982 and shaded the recessions in grey (see Figure 1). The pattern is hard to miss. The spread dipped below zero before the early 1990s recession, again before 2001, and again before the 2007–09 downturn. It also dipped briefly before 2020, although that recession came from a pandemic that no yield curve could have predicted.






Figure 1



The signal isn’t a stopwatch. Recessions tended to show up months, sometimes a year or more, after the inversion began, and often after the curve had already recovered. It also isn’t perfect. The most recent inversion was one of the deepest in the data. The 10-year minus 3-month spread fell to nearly -1.9 percentage points, and it stayed negative until October 2025. No clear recession followed. With only a handful of recessions in the sample, one miss matters a lot.
Considering this, it is worth asking what is happening now. Yields have been climbing, which is a common headline these days. However, the important factor to consider is that a rise in yields only matters if short rates rise faster than long ones. That flattens the curve and moves it toward inversion. If long rates rise faster, the curve steepens, which usually points to inflation worries or a demand for more compensation for lending long, not to a coming recession. To assess this, I delved further into the data and I split the recent moves into short and long ends (see Figures 2 and 3):
Last 3 months: Everything rose by about 0.3 points, and the curve barely changed. The 10-year minus 3-month spread moved by just -0.04.
Last 6 months: The 2-year yield jumped the most (+0.86), ahead of the 10-year (+0.66). Against the 2-year, the curve flattened. Against the 3-month, it steepened a little.
Last 12 months: The 10-year is up about a full point and the 2-year is up 1.2. The 3-month yield barely moved (+0.26). So the curve flattened against the 2-year but steepened a lot (+0.73) against the 3-month.






Figure 2









Figure 3



The two measures disagree because of what happened a year ago. Back then, the 10-year minus 3-month spread was still inverted. Today it’s positive, at about +0.74. The 10-year minus 2-year spread is positive but thin, at about +0.31.
The takeaway
As the previous analysis shows, the curve isn’t inverted. Both main spreads are positive, so the “classic” signal isn’t on. The warning has historically come from the curve turning negative, not from it being low. The direction is mixed. The part of the curve that most resembles the recession pattern, the 2-year catching up to the 10-year, is flattening. The 3-month comparison points the other way. This suggests that something else is going on.
The Fed’s policy rate is about 3.9%, while the 3-month yield is above 4.2% and the 2-year is near 4.7%. Markets seem to be pricing in rates staying higher or going higher, not cuts. That’s closer to an inflation story than a recession story, though I’d hold that read loosely.
It is worth noting that this is a small sample, and the most recent inversion didn’t produce the expected recession. Policy, bond purchases and global demand for U.S. debt can all distort the curve. And the shape of the curve only tells you what investors expect, not what will happen, therefore any conclusion should be a cautious one. Rising yields on their own aren’t a recession alarm. The thing to watch is whether the 2-year keeps closing in on the 10-year and pushes the spread back below zero. If that happens, it might be worth revisiting recession questions.
